content: 1. Trimethoprim can enhance the effects of lamivudine by competing for renal tubular clearance as a basic (cationic) drug. This interaction may increase the risk of toxicity, so caution is advised, and close monitoring is recommended. 2. Ublituximab may reduce the effects of raltegravir and lamivudine due to its immunosuppressive properties, increasing the risk of infection. Therapy should be modified as needed, and patients should be closely monitored. 3. Valganciclovir and lamivudine can mutually increase each other’s toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergy, particularly raising the risk of hematologic toxicity. Alternative therapies should be considered if available, and close monitoring is essential. 4. The combination of lamivudine and zidovudine increases the risk of immune reconstitution syndrome. Additionally, lamivudine enhances the effects of zidovudine through pharmacodynamic synergy, which may be beneficial but requires close monitoring. 5. Zinc can reduce the levels or effects of raltegravir by binding to cations in the gastrointestinal tract. To minimize this interaction, raltegravir should be administered either two hours before or six hours after products containing polyvalent cations. Therapy should be adjusted and monitored closely. 6. Common side effects of these medications include cough, diarrhea, fatigue, malaise, fever (in pediatric patients), headache, musculoskeletal pain, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and neuropathy (including peripheral neuropathy). Other reported adverse effects include pancreatitis, increased total cholesterol, anorexia, arthralgia, chills, depression, dizziness, dyspepsia, insomnia, myalgia, rash, thrombocytopenia, and elevated creatine phosphokinase, AST, glucose, and bilirubin levels. 7. Less common but significant adverse effects include nasopharyngitis, influenza-like symptoms, pyrexia, asthenia, gastrointestinal disorders, lipoatrophy, skin disorders, hypersensitivity reactions, renal failure, suicidal ideation, body fat redistribution, elevated amylase, neutropenia, hepatitis B exacerbation, cerebellar ataxia, hepatic failure, rhabdomyolysis, and psychiatric disorders such as anxiety, depression, paranoia, and suicidal behaviors. 8. Severe and potentially life-threatening skin reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported with raltegravir. Hypersensitivity reactions characterized by rash, systemic symptoms, and sometimes organ dysfunction (e.g., hepatic failure) have also been observed. Discontinue treatment immediately if these symptoms occur. 9. Immune reconstitution syndrome has been reported with combination antiretroviral therapy. This may manifest as an inflammatory response to residual opportunistic infections or the emergence of autoimmune disorders such as Graves’ disease, polymyositis, or Guillain-Barré syndrome. 10. Redistribution or accumulation of body fat, including central obesity, dorsocervical fat enlargement (buffalo hump), peripheral wasting, facial wasting, breast enlargement, and a Cushingoid appearance, has been reported with antiretroviral therapies. 11. Lamivudine and raltegravir should not be used in combination with other products containing their individual components or emtricitabine. 12. Lamivudine is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) that, after phosphorylation, inhibits HIV reverse transcriptase by terminating the viral DNA chain. It is a cytosine analog. 13. Raltegravir is an integrase inhibitor that blocks the catalytic activity of HIV-1 integrase, an enzyme essential for viral replication. 14. The bioavailability of raltegravir is approximately 60% when fasting, with peak plasma levels reached within one hour. Once absorbed, the distribution, metabolism, and excretion of lamivudine and raltegravir are similar to their individual components. 15. These medications can be taken with or without food. 16. Severe lactic acidosis and hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported with NRTIs such as lamivudine, either alone or in combination with other antiretrovirals. 17. Post-treatment exacerbations of hepatitis have been reported in patients with HIV-1 and hepatitis B virus co-infection. 18. Hepatic decompensation has been reported when used with interferonor ribavirin-based regimens. Ribavirin may reduce the phosphorylation of pyrimidine NRTIs like lamivudine. 19. Breastfeeding is not recommended while taking lamivudine/raltegravir, and HIV-1-infected mothers are advised not to breastfeed to prevent postnatal transmission of HIV-1. 20. Pregnancy Category C: Lamivudine and raltegravir should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefits justify the potential risks to the fetus. Controlled studies in pregnant women have not shown evidence of fetal risk. 21. Adding plans allows for the comparison of formulary status with other drugs in the same class. Formulary information may vary and is subject to change, so it is recommended to contact the applicable plan provider for the most current details.
